narrative:
The model predicted a 61% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year, well below the average performance of students who were accepted. These low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly suggested difficulty passing the bar.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 37, it sits almost exactly at the average of previously accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. However, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the negative effect of your class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.8, which is actually higher than the accepted-student average of 3.23, along with your middle-income background, full-time study plans, gender, and race, played only minor roles and were not decisive.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness before reapplying. Consider retaking key courses, seeking tutoring, or enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program that can demonstrate consistent high performance. Raising your class standing and sharpening test skills will directly address the factors that led to this rejection. (248 words)
